passage:
Monday: Alka sent Nikhil a good-morning message at 6:50, as always. He replied at 11:30 with a thumbs up. She stared at it all through chemistry. A thumbs up?
Wednesday: Nikhil was playing football after school and didn't pick up her two calls. Later he texted, "Why do u need to talk every hour?" She typed, "Why do you suddenly not want to?", deleted it, and sent "ok 🙂" instead.
Saturday: At Jasleen's house, Alka kept checking her phone through the whole film. Jasleen asked, "Everything fine with Nikhil?"
"Totally fine," Alka said, too fast.
She didn't say that he felt far away, or that she had started to feel annoying. Saying it out loud felt like it would make it true.

qa.q: What time did Nikhil reply on Monday?
qa.a: He replied at 11:30 with a thumbs up.

qa.q: Why did Alka say 'Totally fine' too fast?
qa.a: Alka was afraid that admitting the distance aloud would make it real, so she covered it up.

qa.q: What could Alka try instead of sending a smiley 'ok'?
qa.a: Alka could calmly tell Nikhil she's been feeling far from him and ask how he's feeling, so they can talk before the cracks widen.

qa.q: How might Nikhil be feeling about the hourly calls?
qa.a: Nikhil seems to feel crowded by constant contact and wants some space, though he hasn't said so kindly or clearly.

grounding: Shows the first cracks in a teen relationship: slower replies, annoyance at constant contact and at distance, and neither saying it aloud.

passage:
Come here, Shalini. You think these phone troubles are new? In 1979, in Aizawl, I, Lalremsiami, was sixteen and Zothan was seventeen. We wrote notes and passed them through my cousin at church every Sunday.
At first his notes were two pages. Then one page. Then half a page, about football. I wrote longer and longer notes, asking what he was thinking, asking why he didn't come by the bakery any more.
Once he sent back one line: "You write too much, Siami." I was so angry I tore it up. But I still wrote him a long note the next week.
And here is the thing, my dear. Neither of us said, "Something has changed." I was afraid that if I said it, it would be true. I think he was afraid too.
So we both just waited. Waiting doesn't fix a crack. It only hides it.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami and Zothan pass their notes?
qa.a: They passed notes through Lalremsiami's cousin at church every Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami never say 'Something has changed'?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was afraid that saying it would make it true, so the change stayed unspoken.

qa.q: What could the young Lalremsiami have done when the notes got shorter?
qa.a: Lalremsiami could have asked Zothan gently and directly how he felt, instead of writing longer notes and hoping.

qa.q: How might Zothan have felt receiving longer and longer notes?
qa.a: Zothan probably felt pressured by the growing need, which is why he wrote 'You write too much', while also being afraid to name the change.

grounding: Illustrates, in an elder's memory, small cracks in a teen relationship: shorter replies, growing need and irritation, and neither naming the change.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Devika used to wait at the village well every evening, pretending to fill water, until Mohan cycled past from his tuition in town. Now she sometimes went home early.

He had started texting her every hour. Where are you? What are you doing? Why didn't you reply? At first it had felt sweet. Now, when her phone buzzed during her homework, her shoulders tightened.

Mohan noticed too. When she said she was busy on Saturday, he went quiet on the phone, then said, "You're always busy now."

"Exam season," she said.

"You used to be busy with me."

Her friend Aadhya asked her at the temple fair, "Are you two all right?"

"We're fine," Devika said, too quickly.

She wanted to say more. So did he, she guessed. But neither of them did. Saying it out loud felt like it would break something.

qa.q: Where did Devika use to wait for Mohan every evening?
qa.a: At the village well.

qa.q: What does Devika's tightening shoulders show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she is annoyed and feels crowded by Mohan's constant texts, though she hasn't said so.

qa.q: What went wrong at this stage, and what could help?
qa.a: Neither of them says what they feel, so small annoyances grow; an honest, calm talk about needing space and fearing distance could help.

qa.q: What is it like for Mohan when Devika says she's busy?
qa.a: He feels hurt and worried about the growing distance, missing how things used to be.

grounding: Devika is annoyed by Mohan's need for constant contact while he feels her growing distance, and neither says it for fear of making it real.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
In Durban, Jamal and Lindiwe had been together since the school play in March. By August, things had shifted.

Lindiwe replied to his messages more slowly, sometimes hours later. Jamal noticed. He started sending more, and checking whether she'd read them. When she did reply, it was short: "haha" or "busy with Nomsa."

On Friday after school, he waited by the gate. She came out laughing with her friends and seemed surprised to see him.

"Want to get chips?" he asked.

"Can't today. Netball."

She squeezed his hand quickly and ran off. Jamal stood there feeling foolish and angry at the same time.

That night Lindiwe lay awake, annoyed at the eleven messages on her screen and guilty for being annoyed. She thought about saying something. She didn't. If she said it, it would be true.

qa.q: What did Jamal suggest after school on Friday?
qa.a: Getting chips.

qa.q: How does Jamal feel standing at the gate after Lindiwe runs off?
qa.a: He feels foolish and angry, sensing the growing distance between them.

qa.q: What could each of them do instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Jamal could say he misses her instead of sending more messages, and Lindiwe could say calmly that she needs a bit more space.

qa.q: What is it like for Lindiwe to see eleven messages at night?
qa.a: She feels annoyed and crowded, and guilty for being annoyed, but afraid to say so.

grounding: Jamal and Lindiwe's replies slow and annoyance grows on both sides, but neither names the cracks for fear of making them real.

Phone hour in the girls' hostel ran from eight to nine, and Farida's phone buzzed at 8:01. Nikhil: "Hey?" At 8:03: "You there?" At 8:04: "Busy? 😕" She turned it face down and opened her chemistry notes. Across the room Irawati raised an eyebrow. "Not replying?"
"In a bit," Farida said, and did not move.
A month ago she had waited by the charging point for his first message. Now each buzz felt like a tap on her shoulder that would not stop. At 8:40 she typed "sorry, studying" and deleted the longer line under it: "can we not talk every single minute?"
His reply came in three seconds: "ok. you've been busy a lot lately."
She stared at the word lately for a while. Then she wrote, "haha no, just exams 🙂" and switched off the screen, and neither of them said what they meant.

qa.q: When did phone hour run in the girls' hostel?
qa.a: Phone hour ran from eight to nine.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling as Nikhil's messages kept coming?
qa.a: She felt irritated and crowded, as if each buzz were a tap on her shoulder that would not stop, though she hid it behind short replies.

qa.q: What small, honest step could Farida take at this stage instead of 'haha no, just exams'?
qa.a: She could say kindly that she likes talking but needs quiet during study time, so the crack is named while it is still small.

qa.q: How might Nikhil be reading Farida's short replies?
qa.a: Nikhil seems to sense her growing distance, since he says she's been busy a lot lately, and he may feel hurt or worried and message more because of it.

grounding: Shows small cracks in a teen relationship, with one irritated by constant contact, the other sensing distance, and neither saying so.
